# Frame — product-process-2026-08

Question (verbatim): "There seems to be a missing step where a problem statement is associated directly to a bounded context shop. Requests are made against a product, not against bounded contexts. A feature can easily cross multiple bounded contexts. Please do research contrasting the product process we are developing against industry standards, focusing more on the modern end of the spectrum with startups tech companies. I don't just want the research based on this comment about features spanning multiple bounded contexts. I want to make sure we have a product process that allows us to make sense of how the product has changed over time, where it is now and where it is going next."

Consumer: the product authority (David), who holds the lead-pm role. Decision served: what the lead shop's product process should be — the artifacts and steps from a request against the product to work in Bounded Context shops — so that (a) product-level problems have a home independent of any one context, (b) cross-context features are decomposed deliberately, and (c) the record answers three questions at any time: how has the product changed, where is it now, where is it going next.

Our current process, for contrast (the shop's definitions on the `rebaseline` branch):
- Roles: lead-pm (held by the authority in person; frames intent, decides value/viability and roadmap priority, checks the PO's output), lead-po (the maker: briefs, product decision records, acceptance scenarios, backlog order), lead-solutions-architect (stack, decomposition into Bounded Contexts, contracts, scenario assignment), lead-product-designer (experience corpus, usability).
- Artifacts: framing (the PM's recorded statement of what a request is about: originator, problem, outcome); brief (a bounded statement of a problem and its scope for ONE Bounded Context shop); product decision record (ADR-style); acceptance scenarios (Gherkin, per behavior, owned by one context); backlog order (within the framing; mirrors the decomposition); decision briefs to the authority; Document History on every definition.
- Flow: request → framing (PM) → brief/scenarios/backlog (PO) → PO output check (PM) → assignment to a context (architect) → BC shop builds under isolation → reconciliation → interaction conformance check (designer).
- Gap the authority names: no product-level problem statement between framing and brief; features spanning contexts have no artifact; no artifact answers "how did the product change / where is it / where next".

Scope: modern product practice at startups and tech companies (2015–2026) — product strategy and vision docs, opportunity/problem framing (opportunity solution trees, product kata, opportunity assessments), shaping and betting (Shape Up), working-backwards PR/FAQ, PRDs/one-pagers at startups, roadmaps (now/next/later, outcome roadmaps), changelogs and release notes as product history, product decision logs, product ops; and the DDD/architecture side of feature-to-context decomposition (features vs capabilities, stream-aligned teams, cross-context features). Empirical/practitioner evidence on what these artifacts are for and how they connect. Not in scope: SAFe-style enterprise frameworks except as a contrast point; enterprise portfolio management.

Sources policy: primary sources opened in full where reachable (SVPG, Product Talk, Shape Up, Amazon/Working Backwards excerpts, Linear Method, Stripe/Figma/Intercom engineering-product blogs, Reforge/Lenny where readable, DDD authors); secondary marked "secondhand"; nothing cited unopened; model knowledge marked knowledge-only.

Confidence scheme: high — several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary; medium — one opened source, or secondary accounts only, or several agreeing sources that are case studies or practitioner report with no controlled comparison; low — recall without a source, or a primary that could not be read. Confidence and likelihood stated separately.

Assumptions: that "industry standard" at the modern end is practitioner consensus, not a written standard; that the three questions (changed / now / next) are answered by artifacts, not by memory.

Banned words: "seat", "surface".

13	# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next
14	
15	## Executive summary
16	
17	*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
18	several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
19	framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
20	secondary accounts only, or several opened sources that each carry
21	only part of the claim, or a consensus with a dissenting opened
22	source; **low** — recall
23	without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
24	marks a quote carried by a secondary account. This scheme amends the
25	frame's in one clause: the frame made "several practitioner sources
26	with no controlled comparison" medium, which would make every finding
27	here medium, since no controlled comparison of product processes
28	exists; the report instead grades on sources opened, primaries, and
29	dissent, and says in Limitations that all the evidence is practitioner
30	text. Confidence is about the
31	evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
32	its own phrase.
33	
34	*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
35	"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
36	kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
37	(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
38	"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
39	sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
40	in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
41	*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
42	and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
43	*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
44	decision. Names that recur: Cagan and Moore (Silicon Valley Product
45	Group); Torres (Product Talk); Perri (product strategy author);
46	Basecamp (Shape Up); McAllister (an Amazon product manager describing
47	the PR/FAQ on Quora); Intercom, Figma, Linear, Stripe, GitHub, GitLab
48	(their own published practice); Bastow (ProdPad); McCarthy (*Product
49	Roadmaps Relaunched*, secondhand); Mehta (Reforge; First Round);
50	keepachangelog (the changelog convention); Charak and Productboard
51	(product decision records and product memory); Wardley (Wardley maps,
52	a strategy-mapping technique); Evans and Fowler (domain-driven
53	design); the CQRS Journey (a Microsoft patterns guide); Tune, Plöd,
54	Newman (DDD and microservices practitioners); Team Topologies (Skelton
55	and Pais); LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum); Lee (a Spotify post-mortem).
56	
57	1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
58	   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
59	   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
60	   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
61	   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
62	   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
63	   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
64	   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
65	   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
66	   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
67	2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
68	   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
69	   (Moore & Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of
70	   success"; Torres; Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
71	   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
72	   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ, which McAllister says "can be used as a
73	   touchstone; a guiding light" during build).
74	   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
75	   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
76	   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
77	3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Moore & Cagan: "most are 3-10 year product visions"), strategy ("Choices means focus"; insights; "convert those
78	   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
79	   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
80	   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
81	   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
82	   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge (Mehta &
83	   Gadiyali) dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
84	   implement the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for
85	   the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened
86	   source.)*
87	4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
88	   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
89	   before the work starts to achieve the first target condition"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
90	   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
91	   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
92	   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
93	   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
94	   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several primaries, each
95	   carrying one element of the claim.)*
96	5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
97	   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
98	   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
99	   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
100	   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
101	   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
102	   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
103	   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
104	   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
105	   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
106	   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that both forms exist, each
107	   with primary sources; medium that keeping them separate is the
108	   consensus — one dissenting opened source.)*
109	6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
110	   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
111	   named owner, and frequency as the warning sign.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
112	   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
113	   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey defines a business-process flow "in a single
114	   place, the process manager" — a saga for the case that "spans
115	   multiple bounded contexts"; Tune: a dashboard is "a composite of
116	   capabilities provided by other bounded contexts", and journey
117	   changes make "multiple business capability
118	   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
119	   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
120	   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
121	   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
122	   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
123	   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
124	   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic the sources name is
125	   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
126	   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
127	   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
128	   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
129	   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
130	   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
131	7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
132	   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
133	   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
134	   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
135	   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
136	   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
137	   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
138	   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
139	   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
140	   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
141	   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
142	   And nothing counts how often a request crosses contexts, so the
143	   frequency the sources call the warning sign is not observed.
144	8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
145	   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
146	   chain:
147	   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
148	   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
149	   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
150	   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
151	   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
152	   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
153	   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
154	   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
155	   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
156	   active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated updates, the
157	   framing it came from, and — attached by `lead-solutions-architect`
158	   — the decomposition: which Bounded Contexts it touches, the
159	   cross-context flow named in one place (the saga or process manager
160	   that will carry it),
161	   and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
162	   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
163	   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
164	   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
165	   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
166	   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
167	   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, a rendering
168	   the basis compiler generates from the initiatives' statuses (owner
169	   `lead-pm`; never hand-edited): Now = active, Next = planned, Later =
170	   proposed; Completed and Cancelled are the recent past.
171	   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, a rendering the
172	   compiler generates from entries the `reconcile-and-close` process
173	   writes when a delivery is reconciled (owner `lead-pm`; never
174	   hand-edited): one entry per delivered change grouped
175	   Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed, linking the initiative it
176	   served and any decision record; the Unreleased section lists the
177	   active initiatives' expected deliveries.
178	   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
179	   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
180	   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
181	   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
182	   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
183	   context, per period, is a rendering from the initiatives' decomposition
184	   sections, read by the solutions architect role as the boundary
185	   signal the sources describe.
186	9. **What this changes in the definitions — one line each, for the
187	   authority's decision.**
188	   - `initiative` typedef (new; owner product-authority; instances owned
189	     by `lead-pm`): the fields in 8(b); the framing absorbed as its first
190	     section.
191	   - `product-strategy` typedef (new; instance owned by `lead-pm`): the
192	     fields in 8(a).
193	   - `brief` typedef (amend): a required `initiative` link; a brief with
194	     none fails its check.
195	   - `lead-pm` role (amend): the strategy and each initiative as
196	     accountabilities; the go/no-go on an initiative as a decision.
197	   - `lead-solutions-architect` role (amend): the decomposition attached
198	     to the initiative; the cross-context count read as the boundary
199	     signal.
200	   - `discovery-conversation` process (amend): the framing step produces
201	     an initiative's first section, not a brief.
202	   - `review-conversation` process (amend): the authority's go/no-go on
203	     an initiative as an outcome it records.
204	   - `po-output-check` process (amend): the initiative as a criteria
205	     source beside the framing.
206	   - `reconcile-and-close` process (amend): a step that writes the
207	     changelog entry for each reconciled delivery.
208	   - roadmap, changelog, and cross-context count: generated renderings
209	     from the compiler, no typedef of their own beyond a rendering rule.
210	   The four PO typedefs awaiting approval stand; the brief's amendment
211	   is the only change to them.
212	
213	## Method
214	
215	Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts: the product-level
216	problem artifact (SVPG five essays, Product Talk, Perri two, Shape Up
217	four chapters, Working Backwards and McAllister, Intercom two, Lenny's
218	template index and Figma's PRD, Reforge and First Round on the
219	strategy stack, Linear Method and docs); the record of past, present,
220	and next (ProdPad, SVPG two, Perri two, McCarthy secondhand, Linear
221	Method and docs and changelog, keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, and
222	GitLab changelogs, Charak's product decision records, Productboard
223	two, Metabase, Wardley); cross-context features (Evans's DDD Reference,
224	Fowler's bliki two, Vernon via InfoQ, the CQRS Journey on sagas,
225	Brandolini via two secondaries, Tune two, Plöd, Team Topologies three,
226	Fowler/Narayan "Products Over Projects", Newman two, LeSS two, Lee on
227	Spotify). Roughly 60 sources opened in full; unreadable: Perri's
228	strategy-deployment post (404; secondhand), Vernon's IDDD chapter
229	(403), Product Roadmaps Relaunched (book; notes from a talk), GitLab's
230	handbook process pages (navigation only), Lenny's PRD guide
231	(paywalled), SVPG "problems to solve" (redirect). Evidence extracted
232	quotes-first; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
233	
234	## Findings
235	
236	### F1 — The product-level, problem-first artifact *(high)*
237	
238	- Cagan, "Assessing Product Opportunities": "I ask product managers to
239	  answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this
240	  solve? (value proposition) 2. For whom do we solve that problem?
241	  (target market) 3. How big is the opportunity? (market size)"; "a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly
242	  the problem that's solved"; "The purpose of the MRD is to describe
243	  the opportunity, not the solution".
244	- Torres, Opportunity Solution Trees: "[a]n opportunity is an unmet
245	  customer need, pain point, or desire."; "The best way to test if an
246	  opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there
247	  more than one way to address this opportunity?'"; "a living document
248	  that should evolve as you learn".
249	- Perri, product strategy: "The target condition helps break down the
250	  Challenge… achievable, measurable metrics."; "This is what the
251	  current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be
252	  measured and quantified before the work starts to achieve the first
253	  target condition."
254	- Basecamp, Shape Up: "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody
255	  knows what it means."; the pitch's five ingredients — "Problem…
256	  Appetite… Solution… Rabbit holes… No-gos"; "Shaped work indicates
257	  what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
258	- Amazon, Working Backwards: "Problem Paragraph: This is where you
259	  describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve.";
260	  McAllister: "Once the project moves into development, the press
261	  release can be used as a touchstone; a guiding light."
262	- Intercom: "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project
263	  brief... It never includes solutions because this comes later.";
264	  "restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the
265	  problem we're solving"; "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by
266	  team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in
267	  turn are broken down into individual releases."
268	- Figma's PRD (Yamashita): "Describe the problem (or opportunity)
269	  you're trying to solve. Why is it important to our users and our
270	  business?"; "Keep track of open issues / key decisions here."
271	- Linear docs: initiatives "express the goals and objectives an
272	  organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those
273	  aims"; projects are "units of work that have a clear outcome or
274	  planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch" and "can be
275	  shared across multiple teams".
276	
277	### F2 — Problem or shaped solution; the decision point *(high)*
278	
279	- Moore & Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve":
280	  "simply providing your empowered product teams with problems to
281	  solve, and clear measures of success"; "The product strategy
282	  identifies the most critical problems to solve in the quarter, and
283	  the product leaders assign those problems to the relevant product
284	  teams through team objectives."
285	- Cagan, opportunity assessment: "the company make a clear go or no-go
286	  decision."
287	- Shape Up, "Bets, Not Backlogs": "Before each six-week cycle, we hold
288	  a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next
289	  cycle."; "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle
290	  to build. If we don't, we let it go."
291	- Working Backwards: "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should
292	  be well understood because it is described in the FAQs."
293	- Linear: "Communicate the current stage of the initiative using
294	  available statuses—Proposed, Planned, Active, Completed, or
295	  Canceled."
296	
297	### F3 — Where it is going *(high for the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened source)*
298	
299	- Cagan, "The Alternative to Roadmaps": "The Product Vision: this
300	  describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is
301	  trying to accomplish. The Business Objectives: this describes the
302	  specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team.";
303	  "It is all about outcome rather than output."; "high-integrity
304	  commitments… for those situations where we need to actually commit
305	  to a date".
306	- Moore & Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve":
307	  "A strong product vision will inspire an organization for many years
308	  (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
309	- Cagan, product strategy: "Choices means focus. Deciding what few
310	  things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't
311	  do."
312	- Perri, "Rethinking the Product Roadmap": "Instead of focusing on
313	  features to be developed, we focus on problems to be solved."; "We
314	  assign a KPI to each team which signifies if the problem has been
315	  solved successfully or not."
316	- Bastow, Now-Next-Later: "an outcome-focused product roadmap that
317	  organizes work by levels of confidence instead of fixed dates";
318	  "Link each Initiative to the OKRs it supports".
319	- McCarthy et al. (secondhand, talk notes): the roadmap is "A statement
320	  of intent and direction, not a promise of deliverables"; themes are
321	  "The problems / jobs to be done / needs of customers".
322	- Reforge (Mehta & Gadiyali): the roadmap is "the sequence of
323	  features that implement the Product Strategy"; "The Product Roadmap
324	  should come before the Product Goals". First Round (Mehta): "Goals
325	  are at the bottom of the stack, not at the top, because goals should
326	  come from the roadmap"; "It's important to document those concrete
327	  choices —
328	  not just that we've chosen to do A, but also to explicitly reinforce
329	  that we're *not* going to do B."
330	
331	### F4 — Where it is now *(medium)*
332	
333	- Perri: "It should be measured and quantified before the work
334	  starts to achieve the first target condition."; the kata's "Sellers call office less than twice a week"
335	  against "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
336	- Bastow: "Now is the work in motion. These are validated Initiatives
337	  the team is actively working on, where the problem is well
338	  understood and the focus has shifted to the solution."
339	- Linear: "Initiative Health shows whether the latest initiative update
340	  indicated work was on track, at risk, or off track."
341	- GitHub changelog: release types "Release", "Improvement", "Retired";
342	  maturity "generally available" / "public preview".
343	- Wardley, "On being lost": map elements are "[v]isual representation,
344	  context specific, position of components relative to some form of
345	  anchor and movement of those components"; "Every single diagram I
346	  was using to determine strategy in business lacked one or more of
347	  those basic elements."
348	
349	### F5 — How it has changed *(high that the forms exist and differ; medium on their separation)*
350	
351	- keepachangelog 1.1.0: "A changelog is a file which contains a
352	  curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each
353	  version of a project."; "Changelogs are for humans, not machines.";
354	  "Added… Changed… Deprecated… Removed… Fixed… Security"; "Using commit
355	  log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea: they're full of noise."; "Keep
356	  an Unreleased section at the top to track upcoming changes."
357	- Stripe changelog: named release lines with dated versions, a
358	  "Breaking change?" column, product grouping.
359	- GitLab: "For each release, the product manager is responsible for
360	  creating the MR and files for the feature release note."
361	- Linear Method: "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and
362	  external communication. Internally, it helps your team to track
363	  progress and reflect on what they have achieved."
364	- Charak, Product Decision Records: "Every decision has a context…";
365	  fields "Name, Date, Status (Open/Accepted/Rejected), Scope, Context,
366	  Decision, Consequences, Review Trigger"; "important for decisions to
367	  be revisited every so often."
368	- Productboard: "Organizational product memory is the shared record of
369	  what a product organization has learned. It captures your decisions,
370	  the reasons behind them, customer evidence, and competitive
371	  context". Metabase: "Institutional memory is a company's collective
372	  knowledge of what things mean, how they've changed, and who changed
373	  them."; "If something is in your face every day, you're more likely
374	  to keep it up to date."
375	- Quackback (vendor): the changelog creates "an institutional record of
376	  product decisions" — the one source conflating the two.
377	
378	### F6 — Cross-context features *(high)*
379	
380	- Evans, DDD Reference, Partnership: "Where development failure in
381	  either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both,
382	  forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts.
383	  Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and
384	  joint management of integration."; Customer/Supplier: "Negotiate and
385	  budget tasks for downstream requirements".
386	- Fowler, BoundedContext: contexts "share concepts (such as products
387	  and customers)… Different contexts may have completely different
388	  models of common concepts".
389	- CQRS Journey, "A Saga on Sagas": "there may be some business
390	  processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in
391	  multiple bounded contexts"; "the definition of the message flow is
392	  now located in a single place, the process manager"; "the process
393	  manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes
394	  messages".
395	- Tune: "The dashboard does not belong to the Review system — it's a
396	  composite of capabilities provided by other bounded contexts";
397	  "when there are changes to the user journey, multiple business
398	  capability teams may need to coordinate"; "constant meetings,
399	  corresponding changes between one or more systems, and teams
400	  constantly being blocked by others are serious warning signs".
401	- Fowler/Narayan, Products Over Projects: "For initiatives that cut
402	  across multiple product-mode teams, it is recommended to appoint
403	  silo-penetrating, priority-negotiating, dependency-managing solution
404	  champions"; "Cross-cutting initiatives are prioritized by the
405	  business or tech leadership. Initiatives don't get their own team.
406	  They are parceled out to pre-existing product-mode teams."; "aim for
407	  two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work."
408	- Team Topologies: Collaboration — "working together for a defined
409	  period of time to discover new things"; X-as-a-Service; Facilitation.
410	  Plöd: "Bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying
411	  boundaries for teams in the team topology environment."
412	- Newman: "Getting service boundaries wrong can be expensive. It can
413	  lead to a larger number of cross-service changes"; a team "decided to
414	  merge the services back into one big application."
415	- LeSS: "A feature team is a long-lived, cross-functional,
416	  cross-component team that completes many end-to-end customer
417	  features"; "Product Backlog Items are not pre-assigned to the teams."
418	- Lee, Spotify: "Spotify did not define a common process for
419	  cross-team collaboration."; "Autonomy requires alignment."
420	
421	## Alternatives considered
422	
423	- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
424	  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
425	  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
426	  artifact. Rejected.
427	- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
428	  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
429	  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
430	  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
431	  roadmap-of-initiatives.
432	- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
433	  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
434	  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
435	  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
436	- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
437	  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
438	  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
439	- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
440	  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
441	  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.
442	
443	## Limitations
444	
445	- No controlled comparison of product processes exists; the evidence
446	  is practitioner texts and company practice, opened in full.
447	- Perri's strategy-deployment layers are secondhand; the Product
448	  Roadmaps Relaunched content is from talk notes.
449	- GitLab's handbook decision practices could not be read.
450	- The proposal's artifact names (initiative, product strategy) are the
451	  sources' most common; the authority may prefer the shop's own.
452	- Residual at the verification cap (round 3): four precision findings —
453	  a quote's page, a co-author credit, a label's wording, a paraphrase
454	  in quotation marks — were repaired in this version without a
455	  further verification round. No retraction was required in any round.
456	- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
457	  product-level artifact slows small teams more than ad hoc splitting
458	  costs them; or an authority decision that the framing itself should
459	  persist and carry the initiative's fields.
460

# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
secondary accounts only, or several opened sources that each carry
only part of the claim, or a consensus with a dissenting opened
source; **low** — recall
without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
marks a quote carried by a secondary account. This scheme amends the
frame's in one clause: the frame made "several practitioner sources
with no controlled comparison" medium, which would make every finding
here medium, since no controlled comparison of product processes
exists; the report instead grades on sources opened, primaries, and
dissent, and says in Limitations that all the evidence is practitioner
text. Confidence is about the
evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
its own phrase.

*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
decision. Names that recur: Cagan and Moore (Silicon Valley Product
Group); Torres (Product Talk); Perri (product strategy author);
Basecamp (Shape Up); McAllister (an Amazon product manager describing
the PR/FAQ on Quora); Intercom, Figma, Linear, Stripe, GitHub, GitLab
(their own published practice); Bastow (ProdPad); McCarthy (*Product
Roadmaps Relaunched*, secondhand); Mehta (Reforge; First Round);
keepachangelog (the changelog convention); Charak and Productboard
(product decision records and product memory); Wardley (Wardley maps,
a strategy-mapping technique); Evans and Fowler (domain-driven
design); the CQRS Journey (a Microsoft patterns guide); Tune, Plöd,
Newman (DDD and microservices practitioners); Team Topologies (Skelton
and Pais); LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum); Lee (a Spotify post-mortem).

1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
   (Moore & Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of
   success"; Torres; Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ, which McAllister says "can be used as a
   touchstone; a guiding light" during build).
   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Moore & Cagan: "most are 3-10 year product visions"), strategy ("Choices means focus"; insights; "convert those
   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge (Mehta &
   Gadiyali) dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
   implement the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for
   the chain; medium on the roadmap's re-typing — one dissenting opened
   source.)*
4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
   before the work starts to achieve the first target condition"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several primaries, each
   carrying one element of the claim.)*
5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that both forms exist, each
   with primary sources; medium that keeping them separate is the
   consensus — one dissenting opened source.)*
6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
   named owner, and frequency as the warning sign.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey defines a business-process flow "in a single
   place, the process manager" — a saga for the case that "spans
   multiple bounded contexts"; Tune: a dashboard is "a composite of
   capabilities provided by other bounded contexts", and journey
   changes make "multiple business capability
   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic the sources name is
   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
   And nothing counts how often a request crosses contexts, so the
   frequency the sources call the warning sign is not observed.
8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
   chain:
   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
   active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated updates, the
   framing it came from, and — attached by `lead-solutions-architect`
   — the decomposition: which Bounded Contexts it touches, the
   cross-context flow named in one place (the saga or process manager
   that will carry it),
   and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, a rendering
   the basis compiler generates from the initiatives' statuses (owner
   `lead-pm`; never hand-edited): Now = active, Next = planned, Later =
   proposed; Completed and Cancelled are the recent past.
   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, a rendering the
   compiler generates from entries the `reconcile-and-close` process
   writes when a delivery is reconciled (owner `lead-pm`; never
   hand-edited): one entry per delivered change grouped
   Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed, linking the initiative it
   served and any decision record; the Unreleased section lists the
   active initiatives' expected deliveries.
   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
   context, per period, is a rendering from the initiatives' decomposition
   sections, read by the solutions architect role as the boundary
   signal the sources describe.

## Method

Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts: the product-level
problem artifact (SVPG five essays, Product Talk, Perri two, Shape Up
four chapters, Working Backwards and McAllister, Intercom two, Lenny's
template index and Figma's PRD, Reforge and First Round on the
strategy stack, Linear Method and docs); the record of past, present,
and next (ProdPad, SVPG two, Perri two, McCarthy secondhand, Linear
Method and docs and changelog, keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, and
GitLab changelogs, Charak's product decision records, Productboard
two, Metabase, Wardley); cross-context features (Evans's DDD Reference,
Fowler's bliki two, Vernon via InfoQ, the CQRS Journey on sagas,
Brandolini via two secondaries, Tune two, Plöd, Team Topologies three,
Fowler/Narayan "Products Over Projects", Newman two, LeSS two, Lee on
Spotify). Roughly 60 sources opened in full; unreadable: Perri's
strategy-deployment post (404; secondhand), Vernon's IDDD chapter
(403), Product Roadmaps Relaunched (book; notes from a talk), GitLab's
handbook process pages (navigation only), Lenny's PRD guide
(paywalled), SVPG "problems to solve" (redirect). Evidence extracted
quotes-first; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
  artifact. Rejected.
- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
  roadmap-of-initiatives.
- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.

## Limitations

- No controlled comparison of product processes exists; the evidence
  is practitioner texts and company practice, opened in full.
- Perri's strategy-deployment layers are secondhand; the Product
  Roadmaps Relaunched content is from talk notes.
- GitLab's handbook decision practices could not be read.
- The proposal's artifact names (initiative, product strategy) are the
  sources' most common; the authority may prefer the shop's own.
- Residual at the verification cap (round 3): four precision findings —
  a quote's page, a co-author credit, a label's wording, a paraphrase
  in quotation marks — were repaired in this version without a
  further verification round. No retraction was required in any round.
- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
  product-level artifact slows small teams more than ad hoc splitting
  costs them; or an authority decision that the framing itself should
  persist and carry the initiative's fields.
